entry: [[Belarus|Belarusian]] author and oral historian who writes in Russian. She rejects the label of journalism; her genre is sometimes called documentary literature, and her works are built from interviews with ordinary people. *Zinky Boys* (1989), about Soviet soldiers who returned from Afghanistan in zinc coffins, led to charges of "defamation" and "desecration of the soldiers' honor." She was sued by four interviewees; three claims were dismissed and one was partially upheld. After political persecution by the Lukashenko administration, she left Belarus in 2000 and lived in Paris, Gothenburg and Berlin before returning to [[Minsk]] in 2011. Her books have not been published by Belarusian state-owned publishers since 1993. She was awarded the 2015 Nobel Prize in Literature and was the first writer from Belarus to receive it.

Prince of [[Kyiv]] (r. 945–972) whose campaigns expanded [[Kievan Rus']] across Eastern Europe. His campaigns in the east and south helped bring down two powers, Khazaria and the [[First Bulgarian Empire]]. He conquered numerous East Slavic tribes, defeated the [[Alans]] and attacked the Volga Bulgars. Expansion into the Volga valley, the Pontic steppe and the [[Balkans]] led him to carve out the largest state in Europe. In 969 he moved his seat to Pereyaslavets on the [[Danube]]. Although his mother, Olga, had converted to Christianity, Sviatoslav remained a staunch pagan. He was killed in an ambush, and his conquests were not consolidated into a functioning empire. A feud among his three sons ended with Vladimir as sole ruler.

Soviet and Russian classical pianist, born in Zhytomyr when it was part of the [[Russian Empire]]. Largely self-taught as a child, he studied at the Moscow Conservatory under Heinrich Neuhaus from 1937. His first recital, at the Engineers' Club in [[Odesa|Odessa]] in 1934, was an all-Chopin program. He premiered several works by [[Sergei Prokofiev]], including the Sixth Piano Sonata in 1940, and the Ninth Sonata was dedicated to him. His 1960 American debut at Carnegie Hall consisted of five sold-out recitals. He favored live recordings over studio sessions and founded festivals in La Grange de Meslay, France, and at the Pushkin Museum in Moscow devoted to opera, vocal and [[Chamber music|chamber music]]. He received the Stalin Prize in 1949 but avoided Communist Party membership amid political suspicion linked to his German heritage.

Family of [[Passerine|passerine]] songbirds (*Hirundinidae*) found on all continents, occasionally including [[Antarctica]]. Swallows are highly adapted to catching insects in flight, with slender bodies and long, pointed wings that allow great maneuverability and endurance. The family includes about 90 species in 21 [[Genus|genera]], with its greatest diversity in Africa, where it is thought to have evolved. Many European and North American species are long-distance migrants, while West and South African swallows do not migrate. The oldest known fossil swallow, *Miochelidon eschata*, comes from the Early [[Miocene]] of [[Siberia]]. In the [[United Kingdom]] and Ireland, *Hirundo rustica*, the barn swallow, is called the swallow.

Large, colorful [[Butterfly|butterfly]] of the family *Papilionidae*, with over 550 [[Species|species]]. Most are tropical, but the family occurs on every [[Continent|continent]] except Antarctica and includes the largest butterflies in the world, the birdwings of the genus *Ornithoptera*. Caterpillars carry an osmeterium, a forked organ behind the head that releases a foul-smelling secretion when threatened. Many species sequester toxic alkaloids from their host plants, making them unpalatable or poisonous to vertebrates. The common name refers to the forked hindwings of some species. Linnaeus chose *Papilio*, Latin for butterfly, as the type genus. The family is usually divided into three subfamilies: Baroniinae, Parnassiinae and Papilioninae. The Taira clan of [[Japan]] used the swallowtail, called *agehachō*, as its mon, or crest.

Indian [[Hinduism|Hindu]] monk and philosopher, born Narendranath Datta, and the chief disciple of the mystic [[Ramakrishna]]. After a landmark speech at the 1893 Parliament of the World's Religions in [[Chicago]], he lectured widely across the [[United States]] and the United Kingdom and continental Europe. He introduced [[Vedanta]] and [[Yoga]] to Western audiences and founded the Vedanta Society of New York and of San Francisco, which became the foundation for later Vedanta Societies in the West. In [[India]] he founded the Ramakrishna Math, a monastic order, and the Ramakrishna Mission, dedicated to social service, education and humanitarian work. An American newspaper called him "an orator by divine right." He is regarded as a patriotic saint, and his birth anniversary is observed in India as National Youth Day.

Forested [[Wetland|wetland]], a transition zone in which both land and water shape the environment. Freshwater swamps form along large rivers and lakes, depending on rainwater and seasonal flooding, while saltwater swamps occur along tropical and subtropical coasts. The water may be fresh, [[Brackish water|brackish]] or seawater. The two main types are swamp forests and shrub swamps. Unlike [[Marsh|marshes]], which are dominated by herbaceous plants, swamps are dominated by water-tolerant woody vegetation such as shrubs, bushes and trees. Swamps filter sediment, nutrients and pollutants from water, and their vegetation holds soil in place. Farmers historically drained swamps for cropland, yet two thirds of global fish and shellfish are commercially harvested and depend on wetlands.

[[Ballet]] by [[Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky]], composed in 1875–76 and first performed at the Bolshoi Theatre in [[Moscow]] in 1877. The scenario follows Odette, a princess turned into a swan by an evil sorcerer's curse, and the prince who encounters her. Despite an initial failure, the work is now among the most frequently staged ballets in the world. Most companies perform the 1895 revival by [[Marius Petipa]] and Lev Ivanov, staged for the Imperial Ballet at the Mariinsky Theatre in St. Petersburg, for which Riccardo Drigo revised the score. The score includes *Danse des cygnes* and the Black Swan pas de deux, which demands 32 *fouetté* turns. Its origins in folk tales and earlier ballets remain uncertain.

Large waterfowl of the genus *Cygnus* in the family Anatidae, relatives of [[Duck|ducks]] and geese. Swans are the largest waterfowl and among the largest flying birds. The largest living species, including the mute swan, can exceed 1.5 m (59 in) in length and 15 kg (33 lb) in weight, with wingspans over 3.1 m (10 ft). Northern Hemisphere species have pure white plumage, while the Southern Hemisphere black swan is black except for white flight feathers. The extinct giant *Cygnus falconeri* of [[Malta]] and [[Sicily]] was the largest swan known. Swans usually mate for life, and clutches contain three to eight eggs. There are six living species; the coscoroba swan is no longer considered a true swan.

Port and coastal city in southwest [[Wales]] (pop., 2021: 238,500), the second-largest city in the country. Located on Swansea Bay, it is the twenty-eighth largest city in the [[United Kingdom]]. Its Welsh name, Abertawe, means "mouth or estuary of the Tawe." During the 19th century it was the center of the copper-smelting industry and was nicknamed Copperopolis. The principal area, the City and County of Swansea, includes the Gower Peninsula.

Ancient geometric symbol used in many cultures and religions across [[Eurasia]]. Its name comes from the Sanskrit *svastika*, meaning "conducive to well-being." In [[Hinduism]], [[Buddhism]] and [[Jainism]] it is a sacred symbol of good luck, prosperity and auspiciousness. It was seen as auspicious in much of the Western world until the 1930s. It was first used as an international symbol of [[Antisemitism|antisemitism]] by the Romanian politician A. C. Cuza before [[World War I]]. After the German [[Nazi Party]] adopted it as an emblem of the so-called Aryan race, it appeared on the flag of [[Nazi Germany]]. Several countries prohibit displaying it by law, with exceptions for religious symbolism, and it remains a symbol of good luck in Asian Hindu, Buddhist and Jain communities.

Nordic country on the Scandinavian Peninsula in northern Europe (pop., 2026: 10.6 million), with [[Stockholm]] as its capital. Sweden has been inhabited since prehistoric times, and a unified Swedish state emerged in the late 10th century. In 1397 it joined [[Denmark]] and [[Norway]] in the Kalmar Union, which Sweden left in 1523. During the [[Thirty Years' War]] Sweden expanded into the Swedish Empire, a major European power until the early 18th century. Finland was lost to Imperial Russia in 1809. The last war in which Sweden was directly involved was in 1814. It is a constitutional monarchy and parliamentary democracy, and it joined the [[European Union]] in 1995 and [[NATO]] in 2024. Sweden ranks fifth in the [[Human Development Index]].

North [[Germanic languages|Germanic]] language spoken predominantly in Sweden and parts of [[Finland]]. Descended from Old Norse, the common language of [[Viking Age]] Scandinavia, it has at least 10 million native speakers and is the fourth most spoken Germanic language. It is largely mutually intelligible with Norwegian and Danish, though this depends on dialect and accent. Standard Swedish evolved from the Central Swedish dialects in the 19th century and was well established by the early 20th century. In Finland, where it is co-official, it is the most widely spoken second language. Swedish absorbed Low German vocabulary during the Hanseatic era and French influence in the 18th century. Its literary tradition includes [[August Strindberg]].

Dicotyledonous plant (*Ipomoea batatas*) of the morning glory family, grown for its starchy, sweet-tasting tuberous roots, a staple food in parts of the world. Native to the tropical regions of South America, in what is now [[Ecuador]], it has been cultivated for at least 5,000 years. Its storage roots vary in flesh color from white to orange, red, purple and yellow, and its shoots and leaves are eaten as greens. Orange-fleshed cultivars are rich in beta-carotene, while purple types contain [[Anthocyanin|anthocyanins]]. Introduced to Europe and Asia after the voyages of [[Christopher Columbus]], it is the world's seventh most important food crop by production volume. It is only distantly related to the [[Potato|potato]]. In North America darker sweet potatoes are often called [[Yam (vegetable)|yams]], although true yams are not closely related.

Family of highly aerial birds (*Apodidae*), superficially similar to [[Swallow|swallows]] but not closely related to any [[Passerine|passerine]] species. Swifts are among the fastest birds in level flight. The white-throated needletail has been reported at up to 169 km/h (105 mph), and the common swift can cruise at 31 meters per second. Swifts spend nearly their whole lives in flight, catching [[Insect|insects]] on the wing, and their weak feet prevent effective ground movement. Swiftlets navigate dark caves by echolocation. Some taxonomies place swifts with [[Hummingbird|hummingbirds]], which share the ability to rotate their wings from the base. About 100 species are grouped into two subfamilies. The name derives from the Greek *ápous*, meaning "footless."

Multi-paradigm, compiled programming language created by Chris Lattner in 2010 for [[Apple Inc.|Apple]]. It was first released in June 2014 and uses an LLVM-based compiler. Designed as a safer alternative to Objective-C, it reduces common errors such as null pointer dereferencing and supports protocol extensibility. Swift was open-sourced under the Apache License 2.0 in December 2015 and runs on [[Linux]] as well as [[MacOS|macOS]] and [[IOS|iOS]].

Structure designed to hold water for swimming and associated activities. Pools may be built into the ground or above it, and in-ground pools are commonly made of concrete, stone, metal, plastic or fiberglass. Many hotels, health clubs and universities provide them, and most use [[Chlorine|chlorinated]] or salt water. The "Great Bath" at [[Mohenjo-daro|Mohenjo-Daro]], in present-day Pakistan, dug in the 3rd millennium BC, may be the first swimming pool. Ancient Greeks and Romans built pools for athletic training. The first heated pool was built by Gaius Maecenas in his gardens in [[Rome]], probably between 38 and 8 BC. Swimming pools became popular in Britain in the mid-19th century, and the Maidstone Swimming Club, formed in 1844, is believed to be the oldest surviving swimming club there.

Garment worn for [[Swimming|swimming]], diving, surfing and other water-based activities. Men's styles include boardshorts, jammers, swim trunks and briefs, while women's styles include one-piece suits, [[Bikini|bikinis]] and thongs. Before the 1930s swimsuits were typically made of [[Wool|wool]], which became heavy when wet. [[Rayon]] was used from the 1920s, and [[Nylon]], which dries faster than natural fibers, came into use in the 1930s. Spandex, usually combined with nylon, was used from the 1960s, and [[Polyester]] is increasingly favored for durable, lightweight swimwear. The burkini, which covers the body and head but not the face, is favored by some Muslim women. Some companies now make swimwear from recycled materials such as fishing nets and nylon waste.

Recreational form of non-monogamy in which singles and partners in committed relationships engage sexually with others. The term was introduced by the media in the [[United States]] in the 1950s. Practitioners cite an increased quality and quantity of sex.It is sometimes linked to the freer attitudes of the [[Sexual revolution]], the contraceptive pill and treatments for [[Sexually transmitted infection|sexually transmitted infections]]. A 2005 report by John Stossel cited research concluding that couples swing in order to avoid cheating. In a 2018 study, 2.35% of Americans identified as swingers. Surveys report elevated rates of sexually transmitted infections among swingers.

Electrical component that connects or disconnects a conducting path in a circuit. The most common type is an electromechanical device with one or more sets of movable contacts. When the contacts touch, [[Electric current|current]] flows; when they separate, it does not. A switch may be operated by hand, as a light switch is, or act as a sensor, as a thermostat does for temperature. Types include toggle, rotary, [[Mercury (element)|mercury]], push-button and reversing switches. A [[Relay]] is operated by another electrical circuit, and a [[Circuit breaker]] is a specialized protective type. High-powered switches require special construction to prevent destructive arcing.

Landlocked federal republic in Central Europe, officially the Swiss Confederation. The [[Alps]] cover much of the country, while most of its people live on the Swiss Plateau. Switzerland has 26 cantons, with [[Bern]] as the federal city, and four national languages: German, French, Italian and Romansh. Its national identity rests on shared history, [[Federalism|federalism]] and direct democracy. The Federal Charter of 1291 is considered the country's founding document. Swiss independence from the [[Holy Roman Empire]] was recognized in the [[Peace of Westphalia]] in 1648. Switzerland has maintained armed neutrality since the 16th century and has fought no international war since 1815. It joined the [[United Nations]] in 2002 and is the birthplace of the Red Cross. Its economy, with one of the highest GDP per capita figures globally, is built on banking, pharmaceuticals and precision engineering.

Edged, bladed weapon for manual cutting or thrusting, with a blade longer than that of a knife or [[Dagger|dagger]]. The sword developed from the dagger in the [[Bronze Age]], when copper and bronze weapons with long, leaf-shaped blades were produced. The word continues Old English *sweord*. In the early modern period, Western swords diverged into thrusting swords, such as the [[Rapier|rapier]], and slashing sabres. Thrusting swords were light and well balanced for dueling and gave rise to modern [[Fencing|fencing]]. Sabres were heavier, with curved blades for cutting at several enemies, often from horseback, and saw battlefield use until the early 20th century. Non-European swords include the Chinese *dao*, the Middle Eastern scimitar and the Japanese [[Katana]].

Large, highly migratory predatory fish, the sole member of the family Xiphiidae. It is named for its long, flat bill, which it uses to slash at prey rather than spear it. Swordfish are found widely in tropical and temperate parts of the Atlantic, Pacific and Indian Oceans, and are a popular sport fish. They commonly reach 3 m (10 ft), and the maximum reported length is 4.55 m (14 ft 11 in). They usually live from near the surface to 550 m (1,800 ft), and exceptionally to 2,878 m (9,442 ft). Heater cells warm their eyes 10 to 15 °C above the surrounding water, which improves vision and predatory efficiency. Like [[Marlin|marlin]] and [[Tuna|tuna]], they are among the few fish that conserve heat.

Indian composer of [[Carnatic music]], the eldest of its Trinity of composers. Born Venkata Subrahmanya Iyer in Tiruvarur, Tamil Nadu, he was trained in music by Adiappayya, a durbar musician of Thanjavur. He composed under the signature Syama Krishna and is known for complex rhythmic cycles (*tala*). He is said to have composed about three hundred pieces, and he was probably the first to compose svarajatis meant for singing rather than dance. His three famous svarajatis, the Ratnatrayam, are sung in concert. The other two members of the Trinity were [[Tyagaraja]] and [[Muthuswami Dikshitar]]. His disciple Alasur Krishna Iyer became a musician at the royal durbar in [[Mysore]].

Capital of the Australian state of [[New South Wales]] and the country's largest city (pop., 2025: 5,638,830). The city grew from a British penal colony founded in 1788, when the First Fleet, led by Arthur Phillip, settled at Sydney Cove. The region has been home to [[Aboriginal Australians]] for at least 30,000 years, and its traditional custodians include the Darug, Dharawal and Eora clans. After World War II mass migration made Sydney multicultural, and by 2021 over 40% of its population was born overseas. Landmarks include the [[Sydney Harbour Bridge]] and the World Heritage-listed [[Sydney Opera House]]. The city hosted the 2000 Summer Olympics.
